chapter: Basie band: origins, sound and style
title: Southwest sound versus East and West Coast
summary: Regional feeling shapes the sound: southwest simplicity and happiness, laid-back LA, sophisticated East Coast.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Let me ask you both to kind of chime in on this question. You know the Basie sound is a sound that comes out of the southwest. And people say that that sound is different than the sound that was coming off the east coast or the west coast for that matter. How do you think the sound was different, or the feel, or the tunes that you played, or the way that the tunes was structured was different than the east coast, let’s say.

Well I think when you speak of different sounds evolving from different sections of the country, I think you have to take into account the whole, the feeling that people are giving out in that area. And music, especially this music, being a music of feeling. When those people come to play, they, all they do is like they’re exhibiting those feelings that they picked up all day long. So consequently, in the southwest or wherever, if you got that southwest feeling, that’s what’s going to come out on the end of that horn, you know. And if you’re in LA and you got that LA feeling, I think LA has always been a little laid back kind of an area, so out there the jazz has always been kind of laid back, you know. The East Coast —no, go ahead, Foss.
The sophisticates were on the east coast.
That music was classy and elegant and elaborately orchestrated, and slick.
So out in the southwest, like simplicity, happiness, that happy feeling sort of a carefree feeling and a looser thing, than the, just like loosening the tie as opposed to it being off.
